questions.q: In this lab's task, what target expectation value is the single-qubit circuit RY(theta)|0> being trained to reach, and why?
options: There is no specific numeric target; the lab only measures circuit depth
<Z> = 0, corresponding to a 50/50 equator state on the Bloch sphere, using squared-error loss L(theta) = cos^2(theta)
questions.explain: The lab defines L(theta) = (cos(theta) - 0)^2 = cos^2(theta), targeting <Z> = 0, a 50/50 state, and tracks gradient descent toward that target starting from theta = pi/3.

questions.q: Starting at theta = pi/3 with cos(pi/3) = 0.5, what is the loss L(theta) at iteration 0?
questions.explain: L(theta) = cos^2(theta) = 0.5^2 = 0.25 at the starting point, as shown in the iteration-0 row of the convergence trace.

questions.q: Across the 3 logged iterations, what two signs does the lesson point to as evidence of genuine convergence rather than a fluke?
options: The parameter theta jumps around unpredictably between iterations
The gradient is exactly zero from the very first iteration
The loss decreases monotonically, and the gradient magnitude shrinks toward zero as theta approaches the true minimum
The loss increases steadily while the gradient stays constant
questions.explain: Monotonically decreasing loss plus a gradient magnitude shrinking toward zero near the optimum are exactly the signature of a well-behaved convergence, as opposed to a barren plateau where the gradient would be near-zero from the start regardless of distance from the optimum.

questions.q: Why does the lesson emphasize that this toy lab's smooth convergence does NOT prove training will go smoothly for a realistic multi-qubit circuit?
options: A single-parameter, single-qubit landscape has no barren plateau risk and no local minima, unlike realistic multi-qubit, multi-layer circuits covered in later chapters
Because real hardware would produce a completely different cos(theta) relationship
Because the parameter-shift rule only works for single-qubit circuits, never multi-qubit ones
Because the loss function used here cannot be generalized to any other circuit
questions.explain: Barren plateaus specifically require many qubits and a high-dimensional, expressive landscape -- a single-qubit, single-parameter case has neither that risk nor local minima, so its smooth convergence doesn't generalize to realistic circuits.

questions.q: Why is the shrinking gradient magnitude near theta = pi/2 in this lab a GOOD sign, rather than a barren-plateau warning sign?
options: Because barren plateaus only occur when the gradient grows, never shrinks

Because it shrinks specifically as theta approaches the true minimum of a well-behaved, low-dimensional loss landscape -- not from the very first iteration regardless of distance from the optimum, which is what a barren plateau would show
Because the gradient shrinking to zero always indicates the model has failed to learn anything
Because any shrinking gradient always indicates a barren plateau, and this lab happens to want that outcome
questions.explain: A gradient that starts large and shrinks only as the parameter nears the true optimum is normal, healthy convergence. A barren plateau would instead show a near-zero gradient from the very start, regardless of how far the parameter is from any optimum.
